newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO HOPES TO START ON NEW DEAL WITH RUSSIA.
newsitem.headline: NATO HOPES TO START ON NEW DEAL WITH RUSSIA.

text.p: NATO hopes on Wednesday to take the first steps towards a radical new relationship with Russia by sealing a deal for the exchange of military liaison officers between their respective political and military commands.

The alliance's 16 defence ministers will hold talks with their Russian counterpart Igor Rodionov focusing on Bosnia and NATO's offer to negotiate a charter or treaty covering all aspects of relations between the old Cold War foes.

In a major change of policy, Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov said last week Moscow wanted to open a dialogue on the charter offer despite its continued hostility to the alliance's planned eastward enlargement.

NATO is adamant enlargement will go ahead, but wants it accompanied by historic new pacts with Russia and Ukraine and an internal agreement on reform of the alliance's command structure to equip it for more Bosnia-style peace missions.
NATO officials expect Rodionov to give tangible proof of Moscow's willingness to trade by agreeing to exchange permanent liaison officers between NATO's headquarters and Russia's Ministry of Defence.
"I would hope that answer would be positive, but we will continue to concentrate on the major tasks," NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana told reporters.
That proposal from NATO has been on the table for months while Moscow growled over the alliance's decision to admit some new members from former communist central and eastern Europe.
Solana was authorised by alliance foreign ministers last week to open talks with Russia on the charter which NATO wants to sign at a special European security summit in Madrid next July.
German Foreign Minister Volker Ruehe said Solana would hold the first round of negotiations in Moscow on January 19-20.
"For the alliance it is important that the Secretary-General focuses the efforts, we want concrete steps as quickly as possible, we do not want to wait until the summit," Ruehe told reporters.
The Madrid summit will invite certain candidate countries, most likely Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, to open accession talks.
NATO officials now see it as inaugurating a new security order for a post-Cold War Europe which will guarantee peace on the continent well into the next century.
On Tuesday, NATO ministers agreed to send a Stabilisation Force to Bosnia to ensure the country does not slip back into war after December 20 when the mandate of the current force expires.
Russia, which was closely involved in the force's planning, agreed to participate. NATO officials say they now expect Moscow to follow that up by agreeing the exchange of liaison officers. REUTER
